More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change

the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

establish the available defence(s) raised in the said proceedings but must also establish 'breach' on
the part of the owner of the vehicle; the burden of proof wherefor would be on them.
(v) The court cannot lay down any criteria as to how said burden would be discharged, inasmuch as
the same would depend upon the facts and circumstance of each case.
(vi) Even where the insurer is able to prove breach on the part of the insured concerning the policy
condition regarding holding of a valid licence by the driver or his qualification to drive during the
relevant period, the insurer would not be allowed to avoid its liability towards insured unless the
said breach or breaches on the condition of driving licence is/ are so fundamental as are found to
have contributed to the cause of the accident. The Tribunals in interpreting the policy conditions
would apply "the rule of main purpose" and the concept of "fundamental breach" to allow defences
available to the insured under section 149(2) of the Act.

driving licence produced by the driver, (a fake one or otherwise), does not fulfill the requirements of
law or not will have to be determined in each case.
(viii) If a vehicle at the time of accident was driven by a person having a learner's licence, the
insurance companies would be liable to satisfy the decree.

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: This case directly quotes and applies the Supreme Court's Lehru formulation on the owner's duty. It holds that when the driver produced a licence with an endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle', the owner was not expected to verify further details.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the single most authoritative statement in the corpus on what the owner must do. It sets the benchmark: reasonable visual inspection of the licence document, not forensic verification with issuing authorities.
supporting.quote: 'When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. ... Thus where the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently there would be no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).'

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured. Even if a conscious breach is established, the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court held that the onus is on the insurer to prove breach, and the breach must be conscious and wilful. The insurer's defence does not defeat the claim — it only entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even if the owner failed to check (conscious breach), the insurer still pays the third party. The defence does not defeat the claim; it only shifts ultimate liability to the owner.
supporting.quote: 'Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.'

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, the insurer must pay the third party first and then recover from the owner under the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner allowed the driver to drive despite knowing he had no licence. The tribunal held this was a fundamental breach but still directed pay-and-recover to protect the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that even the most egregious breach (owner knowingly allowing an unlicensed driver) does not defeat the third-party claim — it only triggers pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: 'Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had only an LMV licence but was driving a maxi cab (transport vehicle). The insurer proved the breach but was directed to pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the principle to cases where the licence exists but is for the wrong class of vehicle. The owner's failure to check the appropriate endorsement is a breach, but still does not defeat the third-party claim.
supporting.quote: 'The insurer and insured are bound by the conditions enumerated in the Policy and the insurer is not liable to the insured if there is violation of Policy conditions. ... The doctrine of pay and recover has been recognised by the Supreme Court.'

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held a valid LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable, rejecting the defence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Limits the scope of 'breach' — where the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle, the absence of a commercial endorsement does not let the insurer off the hook. This narrows what the owner must check.
supporting.quote: 'Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.'

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability, especially where the licence was subsequently renewed.
supporting.fact_alignment: The drivers held valid licences that had expired before the accident but were renewed afterwards. The court held the insurer liable, finding no wilful breach by the owner.
supporting.why_it_matters: Distinguishes between 'no licence at all' and 'licence expired but later renewed'. The owner's failure to check the expiry date is less serious and does not defeat the claim.
supporting.quote: 'The insurers in both cases have failed to establish before the Tribunal that there was a wilful breach of the condition of the policy and that the insured had placed the vehicle in the hands of a person who did not hold an effective driving licence on the date of accident.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The licence expired on 30.04.2008, the accident was on 02.07.2008, and renewal was on 04.07.2008. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even when the owner entrusts the vehicle to a driver whose licence has lapsed beyond the 30-day grace period, the insurer still pays the third party and recovers from the owner.
supporting.quote: 'Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.'

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision confirming that the pay-and-recover principle applies regardless of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the broadest statement of the rule: the insurer's defence of breach (including licence breach) never defeats the third-party claim. The only exception is fraud/collusion.
supporting.quote: 'Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved.'

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh principles (including pay-and-recover) apply only to third-party claims under Section 149, not to own-damage claims. A fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing insurer will cite this to argue that in own-damage claims (where the owner sues the insurer for damage to the vehicle itself), the owner's failure to check a fake licence is fatal — the insurer owes nothing and there is no pay-and-recover.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly limits its holding to non-third-party claims. In third-party claims (injury/death to a victim), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover principle apply fully. The client's case involves a third-party claim, so Laxmi Narain Dhut is distinguishable on its facts.
adverse.quote: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.'

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that the owner committed a fundamental breach by allowing an unlicensed driver, and therefore the insurer owes nothing to the owner. This is accurate as between insurer and owner.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The same judgment then orders pay-and-recover in favour of the third party. The insurer's defence succeeds against the owner but does not defeat the third-party claim. The client (if a third-party claimant) is protected.
adverse.quote: 'Hence, it is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability.' [But then the tribunal orders pay-and-recover anyway.]

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: For driving a goods carriage carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving licence is mandatory. The absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that the owner had a heightened duty to check for special endorsements when the vehicle carries hazardous goods. If the owner failed to check for the special endorsement under Rule 132 CMVR, the breach is clear.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This applies only where the vehicle carries dangerous/hazardous goods (a tanker). For ordinary vehicles, no special endorsement is required. The owner's duty is limited to checking that the licence covers the class of vehicle being driven.
adverse.quote: 'As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9.'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the badge/authorisation for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that the owner should have checked whether the driver had the appropriate endorsement/badge for the specific type of vehicle. Failure to do so is a breach.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The same judgment orders pay-and-recover. The breach is established but does not defeat the third-party claim. Moreover, S.Iyyapan (doc_032) partially overrules this position for LMV/commercial vehicle distinctions.
adverse.quote: 'The absence of any endorsement in the driving licence as to the issuance of authorisation to drive the transport vehicle and non-mention of allotment of badge number clearly shows that the 3rd Respondent was not in possession of a valid driving licence.'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
adverse.principle: When a licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal, so the driver had no valid licence on the accident date.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that the owner should have checked the validity period of the licence. If the licence had expired more than 30 days before, the owner ought to have known the driver was unlicensed.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The same judgment orders pay-and-recover. The breach is established but the third-party claim is still paid. The owner's failure to check the expiry date is a breach vis-à-vis the insurer but does not defeat the claim.
adverse.quote: 'The owner of motor vehicle, in terms of Section 5 of the Act, has a responsibility to see that no vehicle is driven by a person, who does not satisfy the provisions of Sections 3 or 4 of the Act.'

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the claimant himself was driving without a licence, the insurer will argue contributory negligence to reduce the award. This is not about the owner's duty to check but about the claimant's own conduct.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This applies only where the claimant/victim was the unlicensed driver. It does not apply where the victim is a third party (pedestrian, passenger, or other vehicle occupant) and the driver employed by the owner was unlicensed.
adverse.quote: 'The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW-1 Kamal who categorically deposed ... he did not have DL at the time of accident.'

priority_arguments: The owner's duty is limited to checking whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine — the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO (Lehru principle, cited in doc_027).

Even if the owner failed to check or knowingly allowed an unlicensed driver, the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant and can only recover from the owner afterwards (pay-and-recover). This is settled law across doc_024, doc_033, doc_025, doc_035, doc_003.
The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured — the insurer bears the burden of proving this (doc_033, doc_025).
Where the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle but lacks a commercial endorsement, the insurer cannot avoid liability at all (doc_032 — S.Iyyapan, Supreme Court).
An expired licence that is later renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach if the driver was not disqualified from holding a licence (doc_034).
The only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: In own-damage claims (not third-party), the insurer can repudiate entirely if the licence is fake — Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) is high-risk for such cases.
If the vehicle carries hazardous goods, the owner has a heightened duty under Rule 132 CMVR to check for special endorsements — failure is a clear breach (doc_001).
If the claimant was the unlicensed driver himself, contributory negligence may reduce the award (doc_009).
The insurer may argue that the breach was 'fundamental' and try to resist pay-and-recover — though the weight of authority (doc_025 Full Bench) supports pay-and-recover in all third-party cases.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For a third-party claimant: file under Section 166 MV Act before the MACT. The insurer's defence of licence breach will not defeat the claim; at worst, the tribunal will order pay-and-recover. For an owner facing recovery proceedings: argue that the licence appeared genuine on its face and that reasonable care was exercised (Lehru standard).

caveats: This corpus does not contain the full text of the Supreme Court's judgment in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which is the foundational authority on the owner's duty. However, doc_027 quotes and applies Lehru extensively, so the principle is reliably captured.
The corpus does not contain Swaran Singh itself, but multiple judgments (doc_033, doc_025, doc_035) discuss and apply its principles.

doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is a Supreme Court judgment that limits Swaran Singh to third-party claims — this is a critical distinction that must be flagged in any advice to a client who has an own-damage claim.

adverse.distinguishing_argument: This applies only where the claimant/victim was the unlicensed driver. It does not apply where the victim is a third party (pedestrian, passenger, or other vehicle occupant) and the driver employed by the owner was unlicensed.
adverse.quote: 'The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW-1 Kamal who categorically deposed ... he did not have DL at the time of accident.'

priority_arguments: The owner's duty is limited to checking whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine — the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO (Lehru principle, cited in doc_027).

Even if the owner failed to check or knowingly allowed an unlicensed driver, the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant and can only recover from the owner afterwards (pay-and-recover). This is settled law across doc_024, doc_033, doc_025, doc_035, doc_003, doc_006.
The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured — the insurer bears the burden of proving this (doc_033, doc_025).
Where the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle but lacks a commercial endorsement, the insurer cannot avoid liability at all (doc_032 — S.Iyyapan, Supreme Court).
An expired licence that is later renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach if the driver was not disqualified from holding a licence (doc_034).
The only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: In own-damage claims (not third-party), the insurer can repudiate entirely if the licence is fake — Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) is high-risk for such cases.
If the vehicle carries hazardous goods, the owner has a heightened duty under Rule 132 CMVR to check for special endorsements — failure is a clear breach (doc_001).
If the claimant was the unlicensed driver himself, contributory negligence may reduce the award (doc_009).
If the victim is a passenger in a private vehicle used for hire/reward without additional premium, the insurer may be completely exonerated — pay-and-recover does not apply (doc_028).
The insurer may argue that the breach was 'fundamental' and try to resist pay-and-recover — though the weight of authority (doc_025 Full Bench) supports pay-and-recover in all third-party cases.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For a third-party claimant: file under Section 166 MV Act before the MACT. The insurer's defence of licence breach will not defeat the claim; at worst, the tribunal will order pay-and-recover. For an owner facing recovery proceedings: argue that the licence appeared genuine on its face and that reasonable care was exercised (Lehru standard per doc_027).

caveats: doc_014 (Shivlal) — concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles under the 1939 Act. Entirely about whether the insurer is liable for a passenger whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered. Has nothing to do with the owner's duty to verify a driver's licence or whether failing to check defeats the insurer's defence. Not relevant.

doc_016 (Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State of H.P.) — a criminal revision case about whether absence of a driving licence constitutes rashness/negligence for IPC offences. Holds that lack of a licence does not itself prove negligent driving. This is a criminal law point, not about civil insurance liability or the owner's duty to check. Not relevant.

This corpus does not contain the full text of the Supreme Court's judgment in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which is the foundational authority on the owner's duty. However, doc_027 quotes and applies Lehru extensively, so the principle is reliably captured.
The corpus does not contain Swaran Singh itself, but multiple judgments (doc_033, doc_025, doc_035, doc_006) discuss and apply its principles.

Where the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle but lacks a commercial endorsement, the insurer cannot avoid liability at all (doc_032 — S.Iyyapan, Supreme Court).
An expired licence that is later renewed does not constitute a fundamental breach if the driver was not disqualified from holding a licence (doc_034).
The only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: In own-damage claims (not third-party), the insurer can repudiate entirely if the licence is fake — Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) is high-risk for such cases.
If the vehicle carries hazardous goods, the owner has a heightened duty under Rule 132 CMVR to check for special endorsements — failure is a clear breach (doc_001).
If the claimant was the unlicensed driver himself, contributory negligence may reduce the award (doc_009).
If the victim is a passenger in a private vehicle used for hire/reward without additional premium, the insurer may be completely exonerated — pay-and-recover does not apply (doc_028).
The insurer may argue that the breach was 'fundamental' and try to resist pay-and-recover — though the weight of authority (doc_025 Full Bench) supports pay-and-recover in all third-party cases.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For a third-party claimant: file under Section 166 MV Act before the MACT. The insurer's defence of licence breach will not defeat the claim; at worst, the tribunal will order pay-and-recover. For an owner facing recovery proceedings: argue that the licence appeared genuine on its face and that reasonable care was exercised (Lehru standard per doc_027).

caveats: doc_014 (Shivlal) — concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles under the 1939 Act. Entirely about whether the insurer is liable for a passenger whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered. Has nothing to do with the owner's duty to verify a driver's licence or whether failing to check defeats the insurer's defence. Not relevant.

doc_016 (Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State of H.P.) — a criminal revision case about whether absence of a driving licence constitutes rashness/negligence for IPC offences. Holds that lack of a licence does not itself prove negligent driving. This is a criminal law point, not about civil insurance liability or the owner's duty to check. Not relevant.

This corpus does not contain the full text of the Supreme Court's judgment in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which is the foundational authority on the owner's duty. However, doc_027 quotes and applies Lehru extensively, so the principle is reliably captured.
The corpus does not contain Swaran Singh itself, but multiple judgments (doc_033, doc_025, doc_035, doc_006) discuss and apply its principles.
